paras: The lynching of Richard Jennings took place at Austin, Nevada, early on December 14, 1881, when a party of masked men took him from the county jail and hanged him from the front of the Court-house. Jennings, a miner newly arrived from Grass Valley, California, had been jailed on a charge of shooting John A. Barrett, a well-liked Austin resident, on December 12. The story ran by wire across the country, and Nevada papers largely endorsed the hanging as a warning to armed roughs.

On the night of Monday, December 12, John A. Barrett was shot dead at the bar of the International Hotel in Austin, and Jennings was accused of firing the shots. According to the Eureka Sentinel, Jennings began a quarrel 'for some cause unknown' and minutes later, as Barrett waited at the bar for drinks, fired three shots, one striking him under the right shoulder-blade. The Lyon County Times traced the trouble to a 'difficulty' over faro checks, while the Silver State reported that Jennings had lost at faro and then played on with money belonging to Barrett.

Deputy Sheriff Parish disarmed Jennings and took him to jail, and a coroner's inquest on Barrett met on Tuesday morning. A dispatch printed in Los Angeles that night reported 'strong talk of lynching Jennings', though the Lyon County Times said the talk was not enough to alarm the authorities.

At about half past one on Wednesday morning, a party of masked men, about twenty-five and well armed by the Sacramento account, entered the Court-house and broke down a door with a sledge hammer. They held guns to the head of Deputy Sheriff Jas. Parrish, who was in bed in the room next to the jail, took the jail key from his pocket, and forced Jennings's cell. Jennings was led with a rawhide lariat around his neck to the platform at the main entrance, and the rope was fastened to the iron railing of the second-story portico.

Before he was drawn up, Jennings was reported to have said, 'Oh! my God! Boys, I guess I deserve this.' The White Pine News instead placed the taking at about midnight on Tuesday and said that on the way he acknowledged 'the justice of his doom'. When word passed down Main street, a crowd gathered to view the body and hear the deputy's story.

Coroner Laughlin cut the body down within half an hour, and it lay in the Sheriff's office until the forenoon, when it was taken to the City Hall. An inquest was held that forenoon; reporters could not obtain the verdict but supposed it to be death 'by hanging by unknown persons'. No report of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage.
Jennings's father-in-law sent for the remains for burial at Grass Valley, where Jennings left a wife and four children, or five by the Sacramento report.

Nevada papers spoke for the lynchers' community: the Austin dispatch called Jennings 'a cowardly murderer' who got 'the punishment ... that he justly deserved' and said the act was 'indorsed by all'. The Eureka Sentinel headlined it 'A Terrible Warning to Desperadoes', the White Pine News praised lynch law's 'salutory effect', and the Lyon County Times wrote that 'a vigilance committee may be justified'. The Carson City Morning Appeal joked that his death would reduce 'the expenses of Lander county', while a second Eureka Sentinel piece called the mob's act 'horrible and cowardly' even as it held that he deserved to die.

Outside Nevada the case reached readers through a short San Francisco wire, printed on December 15 in Salt Lake City, Los Angeles, St. Paul and Savannah under heads such as 'Judge Lynch' and 'Lynched in Nevada'. Later reprints shrank it to a line or two, and some garbled it: the St. Paul Globe called Barrett 'Bassett' and the Mower County Transcript reversed killer and victim.

Reports differed on Jennings's identity: the Grass Valley Union first named him Nicholas, a mistake the Appeal corrected to Richard, brother of Nicholas. His origin was given as Cornwall by the Eureka Sentinel and the Lyon County Times, as California of Cornish parents by a Eureka informant, and as Pennsylvania by the Grass Valley Tidings.

bases: A party of masked men took Richard Jennings from the Austin jail and hanged him from the Court-house portico (A2, A4, A9).

About twenty-five masked, armed men (A4) took Jennings, who was jailed on a charge of killing John A. Barrett, from custody and hanged him without trial (A2, A27); local papers framed it as 'Judge Lynch' punishing a murderer (A4, A9).
An independent Austin special to the Eureka Sentinel (A9), the Sacramento dispatch (A4), the San Francisco wire (A2) and a Virginia Chronicle special (A13) agree on the core event.

accounts.gist: The two had a 'difficulty' over faro checks; Jennings shot Barrett in the back; talk of hanging on Tuesday did not alarm the authorities.

framing.detail: Austin dispatches called Jennings 'a cowardly murderer' who 'received the punishment ... that he justly deserved' and the hanging 'a terror' to armed roughs.
The White Pine News, while 'no advocate of lynch law', praised its 'salutory effect'; the Lyon County Times said a vigilance committee 'may be justified'.
The Eureka Sentinel's second piece reported a local verdict that mob action was 'horrible and cowardly' yet deserved.
Papers outside Nevada ran the short wire under heads like 'Lynch Law', 'Judge Lynch' and 'Lynched in Nevada', some garbling names and roles.
